speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the housing program during the last year has generally been very successful, there is still a great need for a more modest type of home which would be suitable for erection in the less populated areas. In the past one of the difficulties has been the reluctance of approved lenders to lend on this type of house, especially in sparsely populated locations.
As hon. members are aware, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been working on the design of a modest house which, while it is intended primarily for rural areas where municipal services are not available, can also be built in the smaller populated centres. The design and brief specification have now been completed and steps to publicize this "minimum" house are about to be taken. This is an example of what may be accepted for National Housing Act lending. Leaflets describing this house are available at every corporation office across the country. Working drawings of this house may be purchased at a cost of $10 a set.
It is hoped that the house will be erected in the more remote areas for a cost of approximately $5,000. Where there are some services in the smaller centres it is hoped that the cost will not be more than $8,000. This house conforms to the minimum standards required for houses erected under the National Housing Act, including a recent amendment which gives more freedom of design in that it permits access to the bathroom from a habitable room or the entrance hall. Copies of the leaflet describing the minimum house are being distributed to all hon. members, and I think they will be doing the country a service if they pass the word around in their constituencies concerning this new and more modest type of home.
I am sure hon. members will be glad to know that there has been a great increase in the number of loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in centres under 55,000 population. The figure for the first seven months of 1957 was 7,531 units, and for the same seven months of 1958 the figure is almost double, 14,581 units. There were over 1,000 more in July, 1958 than there were in July, 1957. We are hoping that this new type of home will be of great benefit to Canadians living in the smaller centres.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the minister would care to comment in a little more definite terms on the C.M.H.C. attitude toward this type of home in the larger centres.
I have in mind the restrictions which exist now and which make it difficult for people in the lower income brackets to take advantage of these facilities. I should like to ask the minister whether or not this house will be available in the large centres, and at the same time we commend him for making it available in the rural areas.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It will be available, but I doubt very much whether homes could be built for this price in the larger centres. The practical need for housing of this type has been in the smaller centres of Canada.
May I be permitted one further question. Have there been any conversations with the lending institutions as to their attitude toward making loans on this type of accommodation?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We always do what we can to persuade the lending institutions to make loans in all centres, and I must say they have been very co-operative. We do believe that the use of this new design will greatly facilitate the construction of new homes in the smaller centres.
Is it intended that the lending institutions will carry the bulk of the financing, or will it be by direct loan from the corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: If the loans cannot be obtained through the lending institutions, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will make the loans directly.

This is very welcome news, Mr. Speaker. I must comment on the remarkable swiftness with

Increased Aid to Universities which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has moved. I think it was about a week ago that the minister told me the plans were not ready, and now they are in form. How far has Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation gone in clearing certain materials for specification in this type of housing? I am thinking particularly of plywood and that sort of thing, which will go a long way toward making this type of construction cheaper. One of the complaints I have had from the plywood manufacturers has been the fact that this material has not been cleared yet through the various testing processes. Is Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation working with the testing laboratory to clear various types of materials?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been working for a much longer period than the last week on the preparation of these plans. The hon. gentleman's question of a week ago was very helpful, but just incidental. I do not have the information necessary to give him a detailed answer to his question, but if there is any difficulty about clearing materials which could be used, we certainly will try to overcome that difficulty right away. I feel confident that there is no such difficulty now.

Mr. Speaker, to assist the universities of Canada, parliament has made provision to authorize payments to the national

speechtext:

I would point out to the hon. member that on other occasions in the house I have been asked about activities of the Canada Council, and in reply I have said that the Canada Council is not an agency of Her Majesty and that the Canada Council Act clearly specifies the manner in which the council is to report to parliament annually. The civil service commission reports that a civil servant-not some civil servants- requested leave with full pay to take up a Canada Council scholarship of $4,000 for an academic year. The commission advises that it has no fixed policy or regulation that prevents a civil servant taking a scholarship but that it is a matter for judgment and discretion to be exercised in each case as to whether or not leave with pay should be granted. In this one case the commission felt that leave with pay should only be granted during the summer months, when the individual in question could be relatively easily spared from his regular position, and that leave without pay could be granted during the academic year for which he would hold the scholarship, and the stand he took was that he declined the scholarship on that basis. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING CONFERENCE ON FOREIGN EXCHANGE SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members may have seen in the press statements that during the earlier part of this week discussions were held in Washington under the auspices of the international bank for reconstruction and development regarding the foreign exchange situation confronting India.
The meetings were attended by representatives of the bank itself, and also of the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan and Canada. Apart from Canada all these countries may be described as India's chief creditors, either in the sense that the value of their exports to India substantially exceeds their imports or in the sense that they have extended substantial credits to India for past exports and the debts are now coming due. Canada is not a major creditor in either sense. However, the Indian authorities had advised us that they would wish Canada to be represented at the meetings, and the government accordingly decided to send a representative from Canada to attend. I know the house would approve this decision, in view of the great interest of Canadians in India and the important position which India holds in the commonwealth and in the world.
I am now informed that there was full agreement in Washington about the situation in which India now finds herself and also as to the urgent need to find a constructive solution. The problem arises chiefly from the fact that India's second five-year development plan is requiring more foreign purchases, in a more concentrated period, than India can at the moment pay for. While India has been cutting back both her imports for consumption and her domestic development plans, I am sure nobody, and certainly no Canadian, would wish to see India's development arrested or retarded.
Canada, as I have said, is not one of India's chief creditors either in the sense of accumulated obligations or in the sense of an export surplus. Therefore the Canadian government is not confronted by the main problem facing others; that is to say, the problem of how to arrange finance to cover
4214	HOUSE OF
India-Financing of Development Plan their excess exports to India or how to exchange short term obligations for medium and long term obligations. Officials of the other governments represented in Washington are now reporting to their governments and there seems to be good reason to hope that India's problems in this field for the immediate future may be solved.
We have not yet been able to give full consideration to the report of our representative, who returned to Ottawa only last evening, the meetings having concluded yesterday at noon. However, I think I may report to the house that it appears that in the context of the Washington meetings and the particular group of problems that were under discussion there, the most helpful thing that Canada can do is to continue to provide India with the Canadian goods she may require in her development program. In large measure these are provided on the basis of grants out of the moneys voted by this house under the Colombo plan. To this extent they create no financial obligations on the part of India, nor have they done so in the past. We may also be able to help by accelerating our Colombo plan shipments; and to the extent that this is physically possible, the house may be assured that it will be done.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING CONFERENCE ON FOREIGN EXCHANGE SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's announcement deals with a matter of great importance, primarily of course to India but also to Canada, because there is nothing of much greater importance in the free world at the present time than the effort being made by a free democratic government in India to develop by democratic planning a way to take care of the needs of its great and growing population. Therefore I am sure the house will have welcomed the announcement made by the minister.
The problem of assisting India to meet its indebtedness from outside investment assistance has now been considered in Washington by representatives of the United States and of other countries, of which Canada is one. It is true, as the minister has said, that our assistance to India since world war II has taken the form of grants of capital aid rather than loans. Therefore we are not, as are some other countries, a major creditor of India. I welcome the statement of the minister that this kind of assistance is going to continue-I suppose through the Colombo plan -and I suggest to him that what he has said has underlined the desirability of emphasizing the necessity for capital rather than consumer aid. There has been a move, and I am not criticizing it, in recent months to assist India by sending to her under the Colombo plan consumer goods, but the Colombo plan was originally designed to assist India in the kind 

of development about which the minister has spoken by the provision of capital goods. I do hope that in our desire to help India in other respects we will not lose sight of the importance of maintaining this capital assistance.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING CONFERENCE ON FOREIGN EXCHANGE SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we listened with a great deal of interest to the announcement by the Minister of Finance. We are very concerned that the Canadian government should continue to help India develop her economy. India is, after all, the great fortress of democracy in Asia, and we feel that the Canadian government should do everything possible to maintain the outpost of democracy in that large nation. We believe the Canadian people have sufficient sympathetic understanding of what is happening in India that they would welcome this government taking a liberal approach to this matter and exerting much more effort on behalf of India than has been the case in years gone by.
We feel that the extent of Canada's aid to overseas territories, and especially those overseas territories which are attempting to develop our form of government, should be more like 1 per cent of our gross national product; in other words we should be thinking in terms of $300 million rather than in terms of $30 million or $35 million.

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:

Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Rea in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: Is the minister not going to give some explanation?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not think much explanation is necessary. The resolution is self-explanatory. The legislatures of the respective provinces have passed and proclaimed the legislation to provide for these judicial positions, and the attorneys general of the provinces have requested us to enact the necessary amendment to the Judges Act to provide the salaries in order that the appointments may be made to the offices. Accordingly we are recommending to the house that we be given the authority to introduce the necessary bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few observations I should like to make about one item in the resolution; and I make them, I suppose, because I represent a constituency in one of the Atlantic provinces. In the province I represent, which has a population almost within 100,000 of the population of New Brunswick and where I do not suppose the people are very much more law abiding or less litigious than they are in New Brunswick, there are three high court judges and only two county court judges. In Nova Scotia, which has a population of at least 150,000 more than New Brunswick, and I would think a population at least as litigious, there are only seven high court judges..
It does seem rather extraordinary that in New Brunswick eight high court judges should be required for the discharge of the judicial duties. I understand that the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi has a word to say about the situation in New Brunswick, but it does seem to me there is a great disproportion between the figures for the three provinces. I know the minister's predecessor did not just automatically accept

requests to increase the number of judges when they came from the provinces, but made a very careful inquiry to see whether the money of the taxpayers of Canada should be expended for this purpose. It does seem to me that in this particular case we should have a more detailed explanation than we have had from the minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not completely clear in my own mind on exactly what procedure is followed with regard to the appointing of judges. Possibly I am right in presuming that the only purpose of this legislation is to provide for salaries. However, I should like the minister to tell me whether any examination of the need for the appointment of a judge is made in these cases. There is provision here for the appointment of an additional judge for the appeal court of New Brunswick, and as far as I have been able to ascertain the consensus is that there is much greater need for another judge in the Queen's bench division. If that is so, I wonder whether the minister has looked into the need for an additional judge for the Queen's bench division as against the present recommendation.
As I said before, I do not know whether that is within his jurisdiction. Possibly the purpose of the legislation is simply to provide salaries. Would the minister comment on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
Of course I have made inquiries and satisfied myself, as I have had to satisfy my colleagues, that there is necessity and justification for the appointment requested by the province. In the course of these inquiries I have had correspondence with the attorney general of New Brunswick. My hon. friends opposite will, of course, appreciate that the constitution of the courts is entirely a matter of provincial jurisdiction. It is therefore up to the province to determine to what branch of the courts additional appointments should be made, while we have the responsibility mainly of satisfying ourselves as to the necessity of such additional appointments.
I understand that there was discussion and consideration in New Brunswick with respect to whether the additional appointment should be made to the supreme court or to the appellate division, and the decision was that it should be made by way of an extra judge appointed to the branch of the court exercising appellate jurisdiction. That is my information from the attorney general.
As hon. members from New Brunswick will appreciate, there is in that province a judge exercising jurisdiction in divorce and matrimonial causes who is appointed under provincial legislation with authority in that
Judges Act
field. That judge, Mr. Justice Anglin, has recently tendered his resignation as the judge in divorce and matrimonial causes, and it is therefore necessary to find another judge to discharge that responsibility. The intention is that if this legislation carries the judge newly appointed will assume that divorce jurisdiction. He will be available, of course, as a judge in chancery, the division of the courts in New Brunswick exercising appeal jurisdiction, as I understand it, but will also have jurisdiction in divorce and matrimonial causes.
I am informed by the attorney general of New Brunswick that this matter has been discussed with the council of the barristers' society of New Brunswick and with the chief justice of the province, Mr. Justice McNair, who is of the opinion that this is the best way to handle the matter. I am also informed that the number of judges in New Brunswick has not been increased since 1913, and that the population of the province has increased by about 50 per cent since that time. I am also informed that in 1936, for instance, there were 196 cases before the court having jurisdiction in divorce and matrimonial causes, but that in 1956 there were 597 cases.
I might also point out for the information of hon. members that we are not unmindful of the fact that the appointment of additional judges requires the payment of additional salaries. Therefore hon. members will be interested to learn that although in the past it has been provided by statute under our Judges Act that there will be an additional salary of $500 payable to the judge in New Brunswick who is in charge of the divorce court, that salary will no longer be paid and, with the agreement of the attorney general of the province, the bill to be introduced if this resolution carries will provide for the elimination of that additional salary of $500.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
The minister has given us statistics for New Brunswick. I suppose in making the decision to bring this matter before us he also looked at the case load in the province of Nova Scotia, where there is a very much larger population, where there is only one court, as I understand it, and where one would expect the need for additional judges would probably be greater than it is in New Brunswick. speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-56, to authorize the construction of a bridge across Lubec channel between the province of New Brunswick and the state of Maine.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to authorize the construction of a bridge between Campobello island in the province of New Brunswick and the town of Lubec in the state of Maine. The bill provides that the province of New Brunswick may enter into an agreement with the state of Maine for the construction, maintenance and operation of such a bridge.
An act of the United States congress recently passed authorized the state highway commission of the state of Maine to construct, maintain and operate that part of the bridge
New Brunswick-Maine bridge extending from the international boundary to the mainland of the state of Maine. The matter will be submitted to the state legislature in Maine for action in January, 1959. The bridge will be for the free use and passage of persons, vehicles and goods from a point on Campobello island in New Brunswick to the town of Lubec in Maine.
At the present time there is a ferry service between Campobello island and Lubec, which is subsidized by the federal government under the Canadian maritime commission and the province of New Brunswick. The subsidy is shared equally between the two governments. The service, however, is limited and does not normally operate during the hours of darkness.
The province of New Brunswick has surveyed the area in conjunction with the state of Maine, and they jointly feel that the ferry service should be replaced by a permanent bridge. In part this decision is based on the fact that there are no medical facilities on Campobello island, and there have been many cases where emergency trips have had to be made under adverse and sometimes dangerous conditions. Further, for the development of trade and tourism it is felt that the existing ferry service is completely inadequate and should be replaced by a permanent structure.
The bill does not deal with financial matters; it merely permits the province of New Brunswick to enter into an agreement with the state of Maine, which agreement would cover the financial arrangements and the procedure for construction. This bill does, however, provide that any such agreement is subject to the approval of the governor in council, and also provides that construction must be in accordance with and subject to the regulations for safeguarding navigation.
The bill also provides that Canadian labour and materials to the extent of approximately 50 per cent shall be employed in the construction of the bridge. Arrangements for financing the construction of the bridge and approaches would in the first instance be a matter for agreement between the province of New Brunswick and the state of Maine, which agreement will be permitted by this legislation.
It is proposed that the design of the structure will be undertaken by the state highway commission. However, provision will be made in the agreement that tenders will be called both in Maine and New Brunswick.
As the proposed bridge would be built in the area included in the Passamaquoddy tidal development, which is before the international joint commission, confirmation has been obtained from the commission that the construction of a bridge at this location would not
4222	HOUSE OF
New Brunswick-Maine bridge interfere in any way with the proposals being considered by it. Furthermore, there would be no financial advantage in seeking to merge the proposed bridge with any of the dam structures under consideration for the power development project.
As this would be an international structure, and in view of the fact that the federal government now assumes 50 per cent of the ferry subsidy, the province of New Brunswick has requested that the federal government participate with the province in the case of the Canadian share of this structure. Should the necessary legislation be enacted and a satisfactory agreement entered into between the state of Maine and the province of New Brunswick, the federal government has agreed to share in the cost of the project with the province of New Brunswick. The present proposal is that the federal government will bear two thirds of the cost of the Canadian half of the structure and the New Brunswick approach and that the province of New Brunswick will assume one third of the cost of the structure and approach and, in addition, assume 100 per cent responsibility for the construction of a connection from the highway system to the bridge approach.
On the basis of preliminary estimates the Canadian share of the project would be $580,000, and funds for federal participation would be dealt with under the estimates of the Department of Public Works.
The total cost of the bridge is estimated at $1,050,000. The state of Maine will be responsible for half of that, and the federal government and the province of New Brunswick will be responsible for the other half, $525,000. In addition there is the cost of additional approaches to the bridge on Campobello island, which is estimated to be $6,000, and there is the cost of the road connection from the present New Brunswick highway on the island to the approaches to the bridge, which it is estimated will cost $49,000. The best figure we can get is that the cost in Canada would be approximately $354,000 to be paid by the federal government and $226,000 to be paid by the province of New Brunswick.
This is, of course, simply an enabling bill.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think it will be necessary for me to speak at great length because, as the minister has just said, this bill is self-explanatory and is an enabling bill to give permission to the government of New Brunswick to enter into an agreement with the state of Maine, a measure which is necessary in accordance with article 92, section 10 of the British North America Act.
I suppose the minister has satisfied himself that there is a need for this bridge; in fact


I think he has shown that there is. And I take it he is satisfied that this is an economically justified project, because the share which the federal government will pay will replace the subsidy now being paid under the Canadian maritime commission. This being clear, I think we on this side have no objection to this measure. We are in accord with the principle of the bill and we approve the measure, though we will have some questions to ask during the committee stage.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this bill with a great deal of pleasure and some degree of personal satisfaction. My personal satisfaction I will leave to my constituents to judge, but I do think some facts should be placed on the record to indicate the necessity for this bridge.
As hon. members know, Charlotte, my constituency, is a small county with a population of some 25,000, with three islands, one of which is called Campobello island, which has a population of some 1,300 and which is separated from the state of Maine by a narrow passage called the Lubec channel approximately 800 feet in width, and which is the means of access by the people of Campobello to the state of Maine and to the rest of Canada.
As the minister has pointed out, this need has been served in the past by a very inadequate ferry-a scow pushed by a small motor-which closes down at six o'clock in the evening. Anyone on the island after that has to stay on the island, and anyone who is off the island has to stay off the island. There are no facilities to enable people to to reach the island or leave it after nightfall; in case of illness a doctor cannot be brought to the island except by private boat.
The house might be interested to know that in 1957 exports from Campobello amounted to approximately $1,200,000. In the same year 130,000 foot passengers went from Campobello to Lubec, and 30,000 cars were taken across. Pulpwood was exported to the value of $200,000, and fish to the value of $600,000. As hon. members know, the greater proportion of the total export of sardines by the province of New Brunswick comes from my constituency, and a large percentage of that comes from the island of Campobello.
I think all this indicates very clearly the necessity for this bridge. As the Minister of Public Works has pointed out, this bill simply enables the province of New Brunswick to enter into an agreement with the state of Maine to provide for the construction and maintenance of this bridge. It will be a free bridge, and traffic will pass

over it freely. The people of Campobello have for many years advocated the building of such a bridge, and I am sure I am expressing their views when I say that they wish me to convey to this parliament the appreciation they feel for the steps which have been taken on their behalf. I am sure if this bill passes and becomes law we will have gained the undying gratitude of the people of Campobello and the people of Charlotte county.

This is the type of bill which commends itself to all parties of this house. We know that the bridge which it is proposed to build will meet a very long standing need of the people of the island of Campobello, and we are pleased to lend our support to the passage of this measure.
This is another indication of the excellent relations which ordinarily exist between our country and the United States. The fact that we are able to work out with the United States a method of building a bridge such as this between our two countries is an indication that co-operation is usually possible and to our mutual benefit.
The Minister of Public Works has given us a fairly comprehensive review of the main features of the bill. I notice there is one provision which seems to make certain that the project will not run into such difficulties as have been experienced in connection with a certain well-known project in the city of Hull, namely the printing bureau. I do not know whether or not this is a new pattern which has been set by the government, but the government is certainly tightening its regulations and its supervision to make certain that if anything is done which might be of the nature of a scandal or an extravagant expenditure of public funds, it will be laid at the doorstep of the governor in council and not of some departmental official a certain number of rungs down the ladder. As the Minister of Public Works has explained, the governor in council will have to pass on the plans and drawings, and no subsequent material change can be made without his approval.
I do not know how the governor in council would have the time to supervise this kind of provision if it were in every act and if the government made it its business to carry it out under every act providing for construction, but it does seem to me to be an indication that the government is tightening up on the construction procedures in the Department of Public Works, and presumably in other departments, to make certain that full value is obtained for the construction dollar.
New Brunswick-Maine bridge
However, it will be very interesting in a few years, probably next year, to see whether or not we can have a full and wide ranging discussion of projects that have been built by this government such as has taken place in reference to other projects. I express the hope that in the days ahead we may have a chance to make a thorough and careful inquiry into projects constructed under this administration, following the provision of such a section as is in this bill, to see whether or not there has been inefficiency, extravagance and waste in connection with public funds.
There is a further provision in the bill which I think is most sensible, namely that in the building of this bridge 50 per cent of the content of labour and material in so far as may be practicable shall be Canadian. I think when we are building a bridge in conjunction with the United States it is only reasonable to say that 50 per cent of the labour force will be Canadian, if that is practicable, and also that 50 per cent of the material content shall also be of Canadian origin.
We are very pleased to support this bill, and we feel that it will prove of great value to the people of New Brunswick, to the residents of Maine and to Canadians and Americans generally in the years ahead.
Mr. G. R. McWilliam (Norlhumberland-
Miramichi): Mr. Speaker, the minister has said that this bill is enabling legislation. Like the hon. member for Charlotte, I say this bill is very welcome, particularly to the people of the southwest corner of the province and the people of Campobello island. I think the population figure is some 1,176. The hon. member for Charlotte gave statistics as to the amount of traffic and the volume of fish taken across Campobello island to the mainland and to the state of Maine.
While I support this bill, when I looked at the map the thought occurred to me to ask whether much consideration was given to the fact that perhaps in the days to come there may be a connecting link from the mainland of New Brunswick to the state of Maine by means of bridges or causeways across the islands in this part of the province. If that should come about it would seem to me it would be more practicable to build the bridge from Deer island to Eastport, Maine. Deer island lies fairly close to the state of Maine, but not as close as Campobello. On the other hand it is much closer to the mainland of New Brunswick, as the main part of Charlotte county.
Be that as it may, I do not offer it as anything that can be regarded as an attempt

New Brunswick-Maine bridge to object to the present bill. As I said before, I think everybody is in favour of it, and it is a bridge that is badly needed. When the bill is in committee I may have one or two observations to make. Perhaps at that time the minister may give us something more definite as to how the cost is to be shared. I did not quite catch his figures in his opening remarks. However, we can ascertain that when the bill is studied clause by clause.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. Brooks (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to hold up the passage of this bill. Like the hon. member who has just spoken and also the hon. member for Charlotte, we in New Brunswick are very much interested with the construction of this bridge from Campobello island across Lubec channel.
The hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi spoke about connecting all the islands with Eastport or some other point in Maine. Of course this is a good start along that line, and it may be practicable in future years. If it is I am sure the present government will give it every consideration. It would have to be very carefully studied as a matter of course.
I am very happy indeed that the people of those three islands, Grand Manan, Deer island and Campobello island, have been recognized by the proposed construction of this bridge. In days gone by there has been excellent water transportation between Saint John and St. Andrews and the islands. No doubt that will still be continued, but this bridge means very much to the people of Campobello. I have recommended it in the past and I was very pleased indeed to give what assistance I could to the hon. member for Charlotte in his advocacy of this bridge.
Campobello island has had quite an interesting history. As a matter of fact all the three islands there of which we are very proud have a long and interesting history. They are very important, too, as part of the great fishing industry of the bay of Fundy. Campobello, as you know, was the summer home of the late President Roosevelt. I have not the least doubt that the construction of this bridge from Lubec to Campobello will bring about a very extensive tourist traffic from the mainland to the island. But more particularly it will be a great convenience to the people on Campobello island who, as was clearly stated by the minister and also by the hon. member for Charlotte, become isolated after certain hours of the day and the people also have not the necessary conveniences which people in other parts of New Brunswick, or in other parts of Canada have.
As I said a moment ago, I am very happy that this bridge is to be constructed and that

Mr. Speaker, I too am not anxious either to oppose or hold up the bill. However, I do not think this is as routine a bill as some previous speakers have indicated. Therefore I hope when the minister replies he will indicate whether or not a new policy is developing in this respect.

Marie, Michigan, and so far it has not been possible to finance the bridge under the normal pattern that has prevailed at Niagara Falls, Brockville and other locations with which I am familiar. That pattern is that a private company usually arranges to obtain tax-free bond money from United States investors. The bonds are amortized over a period of years, and after they are paid off the bridge then reverts to the ownership of the people of the United States and Canada on a 50-50 basis. That has been the standard pattern. In the Rainy River district we have struggled valiantly to try to develop that kind of project, but we are having difficulty. Tenders were called two or three months ago and the costs were considerably greater than those estimated by the consulting engineers. That has caused a delay.
I think it is very important for people all across Canada to find out from the minister to what extent there are precedents for this type of federal contribution. We would be particularly happy to know that representations could be made from now on for federal contributions to bridges which have already been given approval in principle by the house but have not yet been constructed. I am thinking of the proposed bridges at Sault Ste. Marie and between Baudette, Minnesota, and Rainy River.

Additional placement officers have been appointed and there are now six regional placement officers and a senior placement officer at headquarters to carry on this important work. The placement officers are largely concerned with the problem of selection of suitable Indians for employment in urban centres. Rural placement has not been overlooked and the fur supervisors employed by the branch were recently reclassified as field officers with the added responsibility of assisting in placement work in rural areas.
Up to the present emphasis has been placed on careful selection of Indians where individual placements are concerned and this policy necessarily should continue for some time to come. In other words, we have emphasized policy rather than the quantity of candidates placed on the grounds that they must prove their worth to employers as well as their adaptability in the non-Indian communities so that those who come after may find ready acceptance by the employer and the community generally. In addition, it has been necessary to develop procedures to recruit and train staff and to establish liaison with employment agencies and employers generally.
From April, 1957 to July, 1958 there is a record of 150 Indians successfully placed in permanent urban employment, of whom 117 were in skilled trades. Our records also show group placements of 788 Indians in agriculture, construction, road-clearing and lumbering. These figures represent only the employment achievements of the new program in its first year of operation. It should be understood that a large number of Indians continue to find work on their own initiative and through the assistance of the Indian agency organization in the field and are not included in these figures.
I should mention that the education division of the Indian affairs branch has been instrumental in providing vocational training and in arranging on-the-job training, and that the results of courses in carpentry and other technical trades have been encouraging. For example, of 29 graduates from the Vancouver vocational institute referred for placement, 26 were successfully placed in permanent employment. The practice of developing the educational standards and technical skills of Indians to fit them for employment in trades which provide greater opportunities will be continued and expanded as time goes on.
I should like to refer briefly to a few group placement projects which will illustrate the

progress made in this field. For several years there has been an influx of Indians to southern Alberta to assist in the cultivation and harvesting of beet crops. The numbers have increased each year. Last year approximately 600 were employed and this year the objective is to recruit 1,000 Indians, not only from northern Alberta but from Saskatchewan. Arrangements were carried on through liaison with the national employment service which was responsible for the actual movement of the Indians.
Last winter through co-operation with the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Department of Public Works the Indian affairs branch supervised the clearing of 24 miles of right of way between Fort Rae and Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories. One hundred and twenty Indians were employed at one stage or another and earned a total of $58,000. This was of great assistance in reducing the number of relief recipients in the area. In addition, 250 Indians were employed by a private contractor in clearing work in the same general area. In both cases the Indians' work performance was reported to be very satisfactory.
Substantial numbers of Indians are employed in the International Nickel project at Thompson, Manitoba and an Indian community has grown up at Schefferville, Quebec, the centre of the important iron ore project there. Elsewhere Indians continue to be employed in mining operations, both above and below ground, and in railway construction and maintenance, as well as in many urban occupations.
Employment opportunities are of course dependent to a considerable extent on the general level of business activity and we look forward to an increase in the number of Indians employed off reserves during the forthcoming year. The goodwill and support of employers are most important in expanding the placement program. In this regard I feel I should mention a letter received a few days ago from a mine manager in the province of Quebec who, on the basis of successful employment of Indians in his mine, has asked our assistance in referring to him an Indian who could be trained for a supervisory position in that mine. This is only one instance of the results which can be expected through confidence gained from satisfactory experience with Indian labour. It is anticipated that as this program develops there will be increasing recognition of the important contribution which the Indian labour force can make to the development and expansion of the Canadian economy in a wider range of pursuits and occupations.

I should also refer to the questions asked by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria with regard to drinking water facilities for Indians on the Eskasoni reserve. The department has been seeking a satisfactory solution to this problem and on technical advice came to the conclusion that the only permanent and satisfactory method of meeting water supply needs would be the installation of a water pressure system rather than reliance on drilled wells. As far as Indian affairs are concerned, this being a matter primarily within the jurisdiction of the federal government and also inasmuch as each province deals with some aspect of it we often find that there is an overlapping of interests and a conflict of opinion with respect to the policies and the attitudes taken toward the Indian people.
We in British Columbia have had in the past year a number of interesting articles which have appeared in a newspaper and we are expecting a number of additional articles to appear in another newspaper beginning some time this month, and we also had a report from a team of professors and students from the University of British Columbia on Indian affairs all of which have done a pretty full and comprehensive job in analysing the problems of Indians and making suggestions with respect to Indians.
I hope the minister will undertake to review quite carefully in particular the Hawthorne report and will also, if she has not already done so, make a review of what I consider to be the excellent articles which have appeared in the Vancouver Sun written by the Vancouver Sun reporter, Jack Cahill which ran in a series of eight articles, I believe it was, during the first part of May, and the ones which we expect to start in the Victoria Times or the Colonist-it escapes me at the moment in which of the papers they are appearing-but they relate specifically to the Indians of British Columbia, even though the conclusions drawn and the studies made could be applicable to Indians in other parts of Canada.
Perhaps the most important long range thoughts of the newspaper articles and the Hawthorne report relate to the question of education which I think all hon. members will consider to be of paramount importance if our native Indian peoples and ourselves as non-Indians are going to work better with each other for the common good of both our groups and for the common good of society. With respect to education I should like to refer to one of the articles which Mr. Cahill has written in the Vancouver Sun of May 7 of this year headed "Segregation of Schools Deplored". Mr. Cahill mentions under eight separate headings questions relating to

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration education. Part of them deal with the number of Indian children attending Indian day schools, or segregated into schools which only Indian children attend, and the author points out that there is an increase in the number of Indian children, an increase in the number of the Indian people, and so on. One important point referred to in Mr. Cahill's article to which I am referring mentions this, and this is a most unfortunate and deplorable part of the results of our educational policy with respect to Indians. He says here, and I quote:
Only 387 of the 5,900 children attending Indian schools last year had reached Grade 8 or above. Three Indians were attending university and 86 were receiving private or provincial vocational grain training.
The unfortunate part of that is the very small number in comparison with the total number of Indian children in the schools who have reached grade 8 or grades ab*ove grade 8. There are very few who are in universities or who are taking additional vocational training. I am sure we all realize that until and unless we can make far greater steps in the field of providing facilities for education to Indian children on the same basis as education is provided for non-Indian children we are going to continue to have a difficult time with Indian affairs. I am not expressing only my own thoughts and ideas in this regard, but I am expressing also the ideas set out by a number of people who have studied the matter in far more detail than I have been able to do, and the views, also, of a great number of Indians, chief counsellors and members of band councils with whom I have spoken personally. Their opinion is the same, namely that it must primarily be a question of education in attempting to draw our two groups together so that we may have a better understanding of each other's ways and each other's cultures.
Mr. Cahill mentions a couple of other matters with respect to teacher qualifications and salaries paid under this branch. May I read further from what he says:
Qualifications of teachers of Indians are generally much lower than qualifications of teachers in provincial schools, though it is obvious that they need additional teaching skills and qualities.
With respect to salaries, Mr. Cahill says:
Top-quality teachers are not attracted to Indian schools because salaries are much less than salaries offered by provincial schools. (The top-paid principal of Indian day schools received $4,950 plus accommodation last year compared with top salary of about $7,000 for provincial elementary school principals.)
He points out further that very few teachers of Indian people have any conception of, or have mastered to any degree the

language of the Indian people whom they are teaching. Of course, not being familiar with the language of the Indian people, which is not a written language, and not being familiar with the terms and expressions and what they mean, their attempts to teach English by, as Mr. Cahill says, prolonged experimentation with sounds bring about very poor results. He points out that most of the young Indian population find this lack of good English a handicap in job seeking and in social life. He says further that the Indian education administration is seriously understaffed with respect to regional inspectors. He compares it with the educational staff under the jurisdiction of the provinces.
It has been my contention for a long period of time,-and I hope the present minister will at least exhibit the same zeal and enthusiasm that she used to exhibit on labour matters when she sat on this side of the house and the same attitude with respect to the department under her jurisdiction and specifically the division of Indian affairs- after discussing it with people who have studied this question quite thoroughly, that until and unless we can bring the education of the native Indian children under the same authority as that of non-Indian children, namely the jurisdiction of the provinces themselves, we are going to have difficulties which are compounded by the other factors that Mr. Cahill and other people set out, if they are valid ones. I refer specifically to lower qualifications for teachers under the Indian affairs branch and lower salary structures, and not as much emphasis being placed upon the question of education in the Indian affairs branch as is placed upon it in the department of education of the provinces. Until we can eliminate this overlapping jurisdiction and bring uniformity to the curriculum and to those who are responsible for education, until we can bring this under the jurisdiction of the provinces, we will be approaching the problem from the wrong direction.
In British Columbia for a number of years now we have had an experiment in integrated schools, if I may put it that way, schools which combine under provincial jurisdiction the teaching of Indian children and nonIndian children. A per capita student payment is made by the department of Indian affairs to the department of education for that service. I realize it may be difficult for the Indian affairs branch suddenly to say they were going to abandon the field of education so far as Indian education is concerned and put it in the lap of the provinces. I do not think such an immediate approach would accomplish much. In fact, it might create more problems than we have at the

moment, but we must express and exhibit more than a pious hope that the jurisdiction over education of Indian children is going to be in the provincial sphere. We must have direct consultations with provincial authorities and express to them the attitude of this department and of this government which must be, I think, that the provinces should take over the jurisdiction over the education of Indian children so that there will be a uniform approach, a uniform curriculum and an enhancement of the qualifications and salaries of teachers to make them more equitable, and so on.
This is just one phase of the problem. I appreciate the fact that we can all express the same ideas, and I am sure that mine are not too different from those of any other hon. member in so far as the necessity of more advanced educational opportunities for our native Indian people is concerned. But coupled with the question of formal education there is the question of the attitude of the Canadian people. The attitude of our so-called white people has generally not been a good one toward the native Indian people. In many instances that attitude has been one of paternalism, an attitude of superiority toward the native Indian people who grudgingly accept their position in life as being a little inferior to ours. That, of course, is something that you cannot legislate for. You can pass all the laws that you like about attitudes of one racial group to another, or specifically the attitude of nonIndian people to native Indian people, but that would not have too much value. There has to be a conscious desire to accept native Indian people as equals and that we will undertake to abandon our paternalistic attitude. We should undertake an attempt to appreciate and understand and experience the same feelings that Indian people have. We should try to understand their background, their cultures, their hopes, their desires and aspirations. In turn, we hope that they will appreciate ours.
To attempt to classify Indian native people as something apart from and different from the rest of Canadian citizens is just nonsense and it will not accomplish a great deal. While we have had, as I mentioned earlier, specifically the Hawthorne report of British Columbia, which has undertaken a comprehensive study and analysis of aspects of Indian life and problems; while we have had in British Columbia a provincial advisory committee established by the British Columbia legislature, in addition to those repor-torial and informative type of articles, such as the one I quoted from the Sun, and one which is accepted to appear in a Victoria paper soon, I doubt whether we have had

I am sure we all know that the ideas and attitudes of Indians in one part of the nation may be different from those of Indians in another part of the nation in the same way that the attitudes of white people in the east may differ from those of people in the west or even in different parts of the same province. Over the years a number of joint committees of the House of Commons and the Senate have dealt with Indian affairs, but I would express the hope that one of the first things the minister will do is establish a royal commission on Indian affairs. I would also hope that its field of jurisdiction would not be confined specifically to the problems of native Indians but that its terms of reference would enable it to investigate the attitude of the Indian affairs branch.
If I were to voice the thoughts of a number of Indians whom I know with respect to the Indian affairs branch the chairman would be on his feet immediately to tell me that I was using unparliamentary language and I would be doing so if I were to use the same terms a number of Indian people have used to me with respect to the branch. I certainly suggest that such a royal commission should be established and I hope that its terms of reference will include the attitude of the officials of the Indian affairs branch and the structure, administration and entire approach of the branch to Indian affairs. Even if it is found that the attitude of the branch is acceptable and that its policies are desirable, such an investigation will at least show the Indian people that the government is sincerely interested in their affairs and it will give the Indians an opportunity to express their ideas about the branch.
That is about all I have to say on these two general matters. Quite frankly I hope that others will express their ideas about Indian affairs and offer solutions to specific or general problems but I still do not think this will accomplish as much as an all-inclusive commission on Indian affairs would. I know that the minister simply has to recommend such a move to her colleagues and action will be taken but if I had the opportunity to vote for it I certainly would do so. I know that she would also be taking a long needed step towards complete understanding and obtaining a compilation of the problems and solutions and recommendations so far as Indian affairs are concerned.
There is one other matter I would like to deal with which I raised during the last session when another minister held the portfolio. With all due respect to the gentleman, we always considered that it was more or less

Last session I raised the question of the rations provided to indigent native Indians.
1	placed the schedule of rations on record at that time and I felt then and still do that the approach to the problem was most disgusting. There has been no change in the rations. They should not be considered rations at all. I am sure that anybody who looks at the list will consider that in no way at all could they hope to contribute to the survival of one person. This list is to be taken as a guide of minimum food requirements, and as I recite the items each hon. member can decide in his own mind whether he could expect to subsist on such rations or whether his wife and family could do so.
One adult Indian who is considered indigent and qualifies for this type of starvation food relief receives the following items: Flour, vitamin B, 24 pounds; rolled oats, 6 pounds; baking powder, 1 pound; tea, 1 pound; sugar,
2	pounds; lard, 3 pounds; beans, 5 pounds; rice or potatoes up to an equivalent value, 2 pounds; cheese, Canadian product, 1 pound; meat or fish, $2.50; salt, 10 cents per adult or 15 cents per month per family; matches, 10 cents or 20 cents per month per family; canned tomatoes or tomato juice in 28-ounce tins, 9-I imagine that means 9 tins-milk, 1 pint of milk or equivalent in evaporated milk per day for each child of an indigent family 12 years of age and under.
That is only for one person. One of my friends from the Hazelton band undertook to price these articles for me in the store there to indicate what this ration means in terms of cost. The flour cost $1.92, the rolled oats 72 cents, baking powder 44 cents, tea $1.32, sugar 30 cents, lard 96 cents, beans 95 cents, rice 38 cents, cheese 65 cents, meat, $2.50, salt 23 cents, matches 10 cents, for a total of $10.47 in foodstuffs by way of relief to one adult Indian. On an experimental basis the department has recently undertaken to substitute relief in terms of cash for relief in terms of food. The maximum amount authorized monthly for one adult under the cash plan is $18, for each additional adult, including children over 12, $15, and for each child 12 years of age or under, $12.
It is difficult to find words to express my attitude to this niggardly approach to our Indians. The amount is far less than unemployment insurance and, heaven knows, that

is not ample, but at least the people on unemployment insurance may have been working in some cases and have saved some money so that they can draw on their savings to supplement what they receive by way of unemployment insurance benefits. But many Indians, because we do not accept them in all walks of society, because we do not accept them in all types of jobs, because their educational background which we design for them does not fit them for many kinds of jobs, find it is not possible to earn the same amount of income in a year as others might be able to earn. Then, in addition to that, they get this grant of $10.47 worth of food to last them for a month.
Any housewife who has gone shopping, as I am sure the minister has on a number of occasions in the corner grocery store or the supermarket, will know just how far $10.47 will go today towards buying food, even if you buy the cheap cuts of meat and even if you shop for bargains. This $10.47 would not last a week, let alone a month. I hope the minister, with her humanitarian ideas, and in view of the fact she is a mother and knows what it is to try to raise children, especially small children, will express some ideas with respect to this niggardly amount of food relief. I hope that this amount will be raised substantially. After all, our native Indian people need to eat, just the same as we do. They have children, just the same as we do and want the very same things for their children as we do. This approach, which has been the rule for some period of time, certainly needs revision. One could talk in terms of trebling or quadrupling the amount of relief given under this program, and it still would not be sufficient.
Before I sit down I should like to draw one matter to the attention of the minister on which I have had some correspondence with the various people in the provincial department and the department of Indian affairs, dating back to sometime in 1955. This matter relates to a road that was built by the provincial department of highways from Hazelton through the Gitanmaax reserve. They expropriated certain lands, many of which were registered by locatees on the reserve. I do not know the exact date of this, but it would be some two or three years ago, that the provincial department of highways paid some $1,500 to this department of Indian affairs. I have a photostatic copy of a listing in which they listed the names of each of the locatees, the station along the roadway, the area and the amount of money involved. To my knowledge, only a few of these locatees have received any of that money up to this date for the lands that were taken.

As I say, I have had correspondence with this department and with the provincial department of highways, discussions on the telephone with officials in the Indian affairs branch, but have not succeeded in bringing this matter to a conclusion. I would appreciate very much getting it straightened up. It has been four or five years now since the money belonging to these locatees was transferred from the department of highways to the Indian affairs branch. Evidently this money got lost somewhere in all the red tape in that branch. I would appreciate it if the minister would try to straighten this out. It is a personal matter relating to these people.
In summing up, I want to say that I appreciate the opportunity of making these few remarks; some of them have been unkind and some of them have not been. I would certainly like to hear the comments of the minister with respect to these matters, especially the question of education and our approach to it. I should like to know whether the approach is going to be different from that of the former administration.

Before the minister replies,
I should like to make a few brief comments.
I do not intend to make a speech, but since I said something about joint education the other day I want to make it clear that I could not go along with the suggestions made by the hon. member for Skeena. It seems to me that the federal government has an inescapable responsibility under the constitution for the education of Indians and for the preservation of certain rights in connection with the education of Indians that would be sacrificed in one or two provinces if education of Indians was transferred to those provinces without safeguarding those rights. I should like to make it quite clear, so far as we in this party are concerned, we stand solidly behind the preservation of constitutional rights in this matter.
With that reservation, I can say that I agree with the objectives of the hon. member for Skeena. As I said the other day, you cannot get the Indian children with other children too early because, as I recall it, even in Wallaceburg where we did not have them go into the schools until they were in grade 4, it was found that it took a year before they felt at home. In Sarnia, however, where the Indians went into the school right at the start they were accepted by the little tots right away and there was no psychological difficulty. I know this thing is going to take a long time and it is going to be difficult. In one or two provinces there is great resistance to this. We cannot have any compulsion in the matter, and we must be very sure we do not do anything that even appears to

I may be wrong about that figure-out of 5,900 Indian children who were attending schools had reached grade 8 or more. there, hoping that the native Indian children would be able to advance into the higher grades more easily.

Is that for British Columbia?
Oh, no. The hon. member was speaking of British Columbia only?

With regard to the matter of rations which the hon. member raised, may I say at the start that first of all we consider that the list which is prepared averages out to about $14 per adult. Even taking that matter into consideration, I might say that these payments were never at any time intended to be the complete living cost of these people. They are based on country food and on the supposition that the food will be supplemented by fish and game, as we know it is. I do not think anyone can ever compile a list that would be absolutely perfect under all conditions. Mr. Chairman, I had hoped that we would have seen evidence of a much broader attitude on the part of the government. This is not a criticism of the government but is a criticism of ourselves as people.
57071-3-269
We have been most delinquent in respect of our responsibilities, duties and obligations to our native Indian people over the years.
Every year the same comments are made in the house, and from the editions of Hansard which I have read it appears that the same type of general discussion has taken place year after year. More than anything the hope has been expressed that our Indian people will be given better opportunities for education and chances for advancement and that they will be accepted by society and improved opportunities for employment and generally enabled to improve their lot in our nation. But although the debates over the years have been somewhat similar to that which has taken place today they have accomplished practically nothing.
Admittedly we have seen a few more Indian children reaching higher grades in school, but certainly nothing has happened which would be anywhere near what should have happened. There have been changes- very slow changes-as has been pointed out, in our attitude toward the Indians, but practically nothing concrete has been accomplished as a result of representations, conferences with the Indians, joint committees of the Senate and the House of Commons and royal commissions. I recall, in fact, one royal commission as far back as 1916 which sat in British Columbia with reference to delineating the boundaries of the reservations or, more particularly, with reference to giving some of the land in those reservations to the C.P.R. Over all these years, however, we still appear to be just on the threshold of hope that something might be done.
This is the most unfortunate aspect of the matter, and as I say, this is not a criticism of the minister or of this government; certainly no more so than it is a criticism of the past government or the gentleman who held the post before the hon. lady or even the minister before him. It is a criticism of our non-Indian society as a whole and of the inability of government or parliament to come to grips with the problem.
If we can spend, for instance, something in the neighbourhood of $16 million per year on immigration-and I am not decrying the fact that we do spend this sum for that purpose-good heavens, can we not spend more than we are spending to take a more definite approach with respect to our native Indian people who were here long, long before the coming of our first settlers? That is the thing that is wrong.
Hear, hear.

Unless and until this minister or this government or any government in

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration office will undertake to do more than merely administer a department, we are going to have the self-same problem continuing and becoming more aggravated as the years go by.

I was unavoidably called away when the item upon which I wished to speak was called, and I will have to send the question X wish to ask the minister in writing.
Does the minister think it right and proper that an indigent immigrant should receive an allowance from her department much larger than the allowance which would be allowed to one of the native owners of Canada who also happened to be an indigent?
I do not think you can compare the two; they live under entirely different circumstances.

speechtext:
I would like to hear more from the minister on the educational aspects of this problem because this is of great concern to the Indians and certainly to those in my part of the country. I have in mind particularly the question of the educational standards. The schools which the Indians attend are being run, so far as I can tell, by church organizations rather than other educational organizations, and less concentration is centred as the years go by on modern educational trends. Therefore, the educational standards of these people have deteriorated as their economic position has deteriorated. If our desire is to eliminate the Indian people then we are probably going about it in the right way because they are losing their identity more each year.
I have had the opportunity, as have some others in the more favoured urban communities, to attend school and to sit in classrooms with Indian children, and I have found that they have made a contribution when they have been able to obtain higher education, not only to our economy but to their own people. Particularly in the nursing profession and allied profession Indians have contributed much when they have returned to their own people. I think the minister must give consideration to this matter and that something must be done very shortly to at least bring educational standards up to the level in the province in which they live and I do not think we should wait for four years before action is taken in this respect.
I would like to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that when I attended a veterans' school I, among others, was asked whether I would take a job teaching the Indian children. The pay was relatively good for the type of employment involved, but our standards of education were certainly not in keeping with those normally required in the


teaching profession. We were merely high school students and were not, in my opinion, qualified to teach Indian children who I believe require more skilled teaching than would be required by average children. We were, however, asked to do this work, which I believe was evidence of the archaic thinking which might be expected if our aim was to dispose of the Indian population rather than to help the Indian people to become assimilated in the communities and to become first class citizens of Canada.
In my opinion the only advantage the Indians have received from us was that during the last war when they were provided with a better type of education if they were able to serve in the armed forces, but we have done very little in the field of elementary education during peacetime.
I do hope that the minister will give consideration to this matter and will have something more to say in this respect. The hon. member for Skeena has certainly given the whole subject a great deal of study and I think some of his ideas should be implemented in the very near future, not only for the betterment of Canadian Indians but for the betterment of the Canadian people as a whole. The Indians form one of the very few minority groups in Canada and we should be able to do better than some other countries with respect to improving the lot of our native population.
I believe I asked the minister at one stage whether any thought had been given to the possibility of increasing the allotments or the cash payments. If an answer was given I am afraid it escaped me.
I thought I had answered that Mr. Chairman. I said it was constantly under review.
Is there any thought of an attempt to make the cash payment coincide with welfare payments to the municipalities?

Yes, this matter is under review right now. I am informed that in one province our scale is higher than that prevailing for non-Indians. In another it is just the same, and in the rest it is a little lower than the prevailing scale.
Does the hon. lady have these figures so that we can compare them?

As you get into the larger families it more nearly coincides with the provincial rate. We do not have any of these figures here.

speechtext: Can the hon. lady say whether it is the intention to do anything about bringing up the standard of Indian education to that of the standard in the province in which the Indians live?
We are working on that constantly. I advise the hon. member that these schools are under inspection by the provincial authorities.

I am very interested in this. I have just been handed this by the hon. member for Skeena. It mentions the rates of allowance to indigent Indians. The maximum amounts authorised are: one adult, $18; each additional adult, including children over 12, $15; each child 12 years of age or under, $12. I think it is disgraceful. If we can pay $65 as an allowance to persons coming into this country who are indigent, and if we can afford to pay $6 a day per person in respect of a certain group who came to this country and lived in hotels and restaurants, I want to protest emphatically against this small allowance made to our Indian population who were here before any of us were here and whose forefathers were here before any of ours. I do hope the department can do something to remedy this gross injustice to our Indian population.
I wonder if the hon. member is aware that this amount is for food only? Things such as shelter, clothing and so on are all in addition.
Even on that basis there is a great discrepancy.
Have you tried living on $18 a month for food?

That is not a hard and fast rule. This is under constant review, and in one case at least it is above the rate paid by one provincial authority. But we are watching the position and hope there can be some improvement made.

I would suggest the hon. lady watches it out in the field close to where these people live. I live very near to a number of these reserves and I have personal knowledge of Indians reduced to such circumstances that they have to go begging to 57071-3-2691
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the Indian superintendent's office and they get a pretty short deal. That raises the question of the acceptance of the superintendent by the native Indians themselves, which is another matter.
You talk about supplementing the income of these people by game and fish, but they find it difficult to do that. At one time trapping used to provide a substantial amount of income to the native Indian peoples but in recent years trapping has declined because of a number of reasons. As far as our part of the country is concerned one reason is that even though they have registered trap lines and are the only ones allowed to trap there, the provincial government has come along and granted timber rights or mineral rights, and when a logging or mining company moves in it ruins the trap line and that takes away part of the income. As far as game is concerned it is the same thing.
Over the years our approach-and it has had a poor result-has been to try to get them to leave their old way of life of being nomads and living off the land and living off game and fish and so on, and to encourage them to set themselves up in our social structure where they should work as much as they can the year round and earn enough to keep themselves and to buy the goods and necessities they need in the same way as some others of us attempt to do. On the one hand, we have been trying to tell them to forget about fishing and hunting as a way of life and to accept our way of life and, on the other hand, we tell them, when they only get this paltry amount to subsist on: go out and fish and hunt to increase it. And in many instances they are not able to do so because civilization is encroaching on their lands.
North of Terrace we have one company in the logging and pulp field which has a forest management licence of over 750,000 acres much of which used to be land which the Indian fished and hunted. Now they cannot get in there because it would be trespassing. Our approach is foolish and I cannot help but take exception to this sort of attitude. I am not being critical of the minister. What I am being critical of is our attitude as non-Indians towards Indians, and as long as that attitude continues we will do nothing to help solve their problems or our problems in relation to them.

I can only assure the hon. gentleman that I am as gravely concerned as he is over the situation, and since the administration of the department is in my hands I will not leave any stone unturned to try to correct injustices.
