Needless to say I would be the first to wish the minister every success in the world.

On item 66, and directly to the point of administration, I wonder if the minister would outline to me something about the decentralization activities of the department? Would she please say something about the jurisdiction of the sub-areas? 1 make no complaint against the minister or the present administration. I want to say very frankly that I have objected to the set-up under her two predecessors with regard to a situation which I do not think was improved very much in the line of decentralization.
In the district of Kenora-Rainy River we have three Indian agencies. They are obliged to report to North Bay. The minister, who has been a visitor to northern Ontario on many occasions, knows there is a distance there of eight or nine hundred miles and I have often felt that this idea of decentralization has merely been camouflage and that in fact it had created an additional post office where mail could get lost and procrastination could set in. The main thing I ask is that the minister should outline the jurisdiction at the Indian agency level for getting certain things done. Would she also indicate what might be within the authority in our area of North Bay without reference to Ottawa? As I say, over the years I have made these complaints to three ministers.
It is my experience that too many things have to be referred from the Indian agency to the subagency and then to Ottawa eventually. The result is that work does not proceed. With respect to such things as the laying of linoleum or putting in a boiler or something of that kind, the decision is received in August and the school does not open until January. I can illustrate that not only in the current year under the present minister's administration but also under the former administration. There is something wrong there, particularly in the construction field. Decisions of importance which involve construction should be taken in the summer holidays when the school is vacant, but the paper work is not completed until well on into August and the result is that the school is disrupted at the beginning of September. I know of at least three instances in the last four years where the schools did not open until after Christmas.

I am not sure whether I understand the hon. gentleman correctly. Is he advocating the placing of more authority in the hands of the superintendent or of the agent, probably with greater spending power at their level? Is that what he is advocating?


Is he advocating that the request should come right through to headquarters?

I am inclined to think that with respect to the larger items the latter is what I had in mind because I get the impression that while they are referred to this sublevel, they have to come to Ottawa anyway. If that is so, why is not some form of duplicate letter sent merely to the sublevel and the Ottawa administration, particularly on construction, repairs and things of that kind, deal with it immediately and not have a new initiating letter from the area superintendent.

Of course, the problem that the hon. member has brought up is not a new one. It has been one that has caused considerable headaches in the department for many years. I do not know to what extent we can streamline the operation to obviate the difficulties the hon. gentleman has suggested but I will look into it. I have not yet had the opportunity to go into some of those details, but I will have a look at it.

I appreciate the assurance, Mr. Chairman. I still recall some experiences in the administration of the post office in the past where there seemed to be too many levels of passing an item for decision and yet it had to come to Ottawa anyway. I am just wondering whether those things have to come to Ottawa for approval anyway or whether there should not be a very serious look at the levels of responsibility. My pertinent question was, what is the maximum authority of the sublevel jurisdiction under the superintendent-I think that is what he is called-without reference to Ottawa?

In my opinion that is ridiculous. There is no point in having a superintendent who is the supervisor of many agencies if his jurisdiction extends only to $1,000, and the correspondence eventually has to come to Ottawa.

If my information is
correct, the public works districts are operated in the same way. Of course, $1,000 does not apply to just one item. For a small contract it does not mean $1,000 a year; it means an expenditure up to $1,000.

If you have to lay some linoleum and disrupt your classrooms it is too bad. If you intend to do that you should do it while the school is in vacation. If the amount involved is a little over $1,000 and it has to come to Ottawa, then the decision is not given until August 15, and my hon.

friend can understand what that means to the administration of the school.

While the minister is preparing to reply I just want to put this on Hansard. This brings to mind something that has given me a great deal of irritation over the years. I refer to the matter of construction. I have been told repeatedly, not only by the construction branch of this department but by the construction branches of other departments of government, that the reason why we have not had much progress and particularly have not been prepared to embark on a building job in the best building season in this country, which is rather short, is that parliament has not passed an estimate. I have not the document in front of me but I am well aware that this is nonsense. There is a clause in the Financial Administration Act which permits a department, once the estimates are tabled in the house,-and normally they are tabled in January-to get on with the job, to get their work done and to get their tenders called. I do not think that the history of parliament indicates that parliament has ever been loathe to grant interim supply, if that were necessary. But it is utter nonsense to hear repeatedly from construction branches of government-and I think this department offends more than most-that the reason they
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration have not a contract let is that parliamentarians have not concluded the session or they have not passed the relevant item in the estimates. The Financial Administration Act provides ample remedy for that and 1 hope the minister will keep that in mind. I drew that to the attention of her predecessors.
I believe we are proceeding as rapidly as possible. I do not think any of our works are being held up at the present time for those reasons.

Item agreed to.
Reserves and trusts-
69.	Operation and maintenance, $327,912.

If the minister has ever had time to look at the proceedings of the estimates committee when this department was before that committee some years ago she will realize that at that time I made a frank confession that in so far as the winding up of Indian estates was concerned it was very badly in arrears and steps were being taken to bring it up to date. What progress is being made in that field?

I can assure the hon. member that we are making progress in this department. In 1957-58, 1,979 estates were concluded and in the same year an additional 702 were opened. The preceding year there were 1,420 concluded and 667 opened.
The minister does feel that steady improvement is being made.
Yes, very definitely.
I am very glad to hear it.

Could the minister explain to me and to the committee what the statutory item, Indian annuities, refers to? I am sure she can do it far more quickly than we can by looking up the statute. Would she also explain what is meant by reserves and trusts? What is in trust?

I do not know whether the hon. member wants a long explanation. As far as Indian annuities are concerned, this provides for the payment of Indian annuities in pursuance of the conditions of any treaty entered into on behalf of Her Majesty or her predecessors, for which the government of Canada is responsible and which is a charge upon the consolidated revenue fund of Canada as provided by statute under section 71 of the Indian Act, which section reads as follows:
Moneys that are payable to Indians or to Indian bands under a treaty between Her Majesty and the band and for the payment of which the government of Canada is responsible, may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.

Would the minister allow a little help on that point? I think I can explain it in two seconds. It is what is called treaty money in all the other provinces and in British Columbia you do not have it.
In addition there was the question of the item in the estimates having to do with the operation and maintenance of reserves and trusts. I am interested in the trust factor. What is kept in trust?

While we are getting the rest of the information maybe I should tell the hon. member that the functions are, first, the management, administration and utilization of Indian reserves and surrendered lands, which includes the acquisition of land for new reserves, and the sale, lease and disposal or other use of natural resources such as timber, oil, petroleum, natural gas and other mines and minerals; second, the administration of Indian band funds and annuities; third, the maintenance of band membership records; and, fourth, the administration of the estates of deceased and mentally incompetent Indians. These are all under reserves and trusts.

For argument's sake, and this is purely hypothetical, if a band in British Columbia sold some timber to a logging company the proceeds of that sale would go into this trust fund and come under the administration of this branch.
That is right.

Is there any provision
whereby the band may prevent the money coming to Ottawa to be held in trust? Is there any arrangement whereby the band may decide that they do not want the money tied up in the Indian affairs branch at Ottawa and that they want to use it themselves for some specific or general purpose?
I am advised there is a section in the act which permits the Indians to handle their own funds but that none of the bands has yet reached that stage.
Who decides when they reach ihis stage?
To some extent they do *themselves.
Again this is hypothetical, but if a band decided that they would use the proceeds from the sale of timber the branch would allow them to do so, or would there be any possibility of preventing it?
It is very difficult to answer hypothetical questions. If the member can give us a specific case, we will try to answer it.

I am sure there are some specific cases. I can think of one near Nanaimo. I pose this question and I am sure it can be answered. If a band decided that certain timber on their reserve would be sold and that the proceeds from the sale of the timber would be kept for use by the band and not sent to Ottawa, would the departmental officials be able to override the wishes of the band and make them send the money to Ottawa?
The funds come to Ottawa and if the band requires money for a specific purpose they make arrangements with the branch and in certain cases the money is used for purposes decided upon by the band.
I think it is getting clearer.

There has to be a resolution of the band. The band has to decide what it wants to do with the money. Representations are then made to the branch and if agreement is reached the funds are handled in that way.
In all cases the officials of the Indian affairs branch are agents acting on behalf of the minister in any negotiations.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: How do the Indians eventually get the benefit of these moneys? Suppose they need to build new houses or want to buy new stoves for their houses and have sold a million feet of lumber from the reserve; how do they get the money back again?

They would make representations to their own band and the band council would decide. The council would pass a resolution with regard to the matter expressing its wishes which would come forward to the Indian affairs branch and the matter would then be dealt with in that way.

Welfare and economic development of Indians-

I believe this item deals with the welfare and economic development of Indians and I should like to express my appreciation of what the branch has done for the welfare of the Indians in my riding. There are still some problems, especially in the West Bay band, but on the whole great progress has been made. But as the minister knows one important aspect of welfare is health, and while I now realize what she said a little while ago, that the health of Indians comes under the Department of National Health and Welfare, nevertheless the problems and the difficulties encountered by Indian affairs doctors, though not under the minister's jurisdiction, will have an effect on

the welfare of the Indians. That is why I venture to bring this matter forward. If difficulties can be created under the health and welfare regulations by a doctor serving not only Indians but in certain cases white patients and if that particular doctor is prosecuted for that under the regulations, then there can be trouble and the welfare of the Indians themselves will suffer. We have an unfortunate case at hand at the moment on Manitoulin island where an Indian doctor has been prosecuted apparently for giving service to some whites. I am sure that is causing a great deal of worry and anxiety and probably some discontent.
That has been settled.

According to the press the case is coming up and the doctor is to be prosecuted. I hope this kind of thing can be avoided because it causes trouble. I am not assessing the blame because I do not know where the blame lies in this particular case but I hope that the two departments can get together and make sure that this kind of thing does not occur.

If my memory serves me well, I saw either in today's or yesterday's paper that he had been acquitted and held blameless because whatever services he had rendered had been rendered with the consent of other doctors who were overloaded and any fees received were paid to the government.

I may be wrong. Perhaps the case has come up. Perhaps the doctor has been acquitted, but the charge was laid by the Ontario college of physicians. What I am suggesting is that surely arrangements could be made in the future so this kind of thing, with all the undesirable publicity, could be avoided.
I think the man was just trying to help out his colleagues in the vicinity, who simply could not handle their patients.
I am sure he was.

I should like to make another comment along the same lines as the comment I made with respect to education. I should like to suggest the same approach should be adopted here, that is that in consultation with the various provinces which have fairly extensive departments of health and welfare an attempt should be made to have these provincial departments look after the health and welfare of the Indians. Having in mind the views expressed by the hon. member for B onavista-T willingsgate-

Twillingate, without any

It is a hard one to pronounce, and I would find it easier to say the unpaid parliamentary assistant. However, with all due respect to the views he expressed concerning the constitutional problems and the hereditary rights of the Indians, we should attempt to move in this direction of having the health and welfare of native Indians under the jurisdiction of the various provincial governments, just as I advocated for education. I say that having in mind the general idea that we will be able to work more closely with each other as Indians and non-Indians; we will be able to appreciate each other's background and culture, and so be able to work together for the general betterment of society.
It is in that light that I am expressing this idea, as I did in connection with education. We should move in the direction of bringing the health and welfare of Indians under provincial jurisdiction so that we do not have two jurisdictions in the field of health and welfare overlapping one another so far as Indians are concerned and their friends who live right next door who are not Indians, and who normally fit into the program of the various provincial governments. I know that at the moment this is something we could not give to the provincial government and say, here, we are going to dump it all in your lap; you figure out a per capita payment and we will pay. It is going to require some extensive discussion.
I feel that the federal department, which now has Indian affairs under its jurisdiction almost exclusively, should take the lead in this matter and express its ideas to the various provincial governments. The hope would be, eventually, of moving in the direction of not having an Indian affairs branch but having the various services administered for Indians on the same basis as they are administered for the other people in this country, working towards equality. I merely want to express the same general thoughts with respect to health and welfare, as I expressed with respect to education.

We have been working on this matter for quite some time now with a view to making agreements with the various provinces. But the hon. member will understand that a plan such as he envisages must entail the province accepting some responsibility.

Could the minister indicate what progress is being made? Is she in a position to mention specifically the provinces which, in a few years, might be doing something?

We have at the moment an agreement with Ontario and 23 out of 26 children's aid societies.
Is there not the same kind of agreement with Saskatchewan?
It is not complete as yet.

I want to make a few remarks on this. I just want to mention to the minister a few of the difficulties with respect to Indians in my territory. She probably is already familiar with them, although she is new in the department. We are feeling, probably as acutely as anywhere in the country, the difficulties that result from Indians moving in, as we desire them to do, to the industrial areas and taking their place on an integrated basis. I want to pay tribute to the officers of the department, particularly the present executive assistant to the Minister of Transport, who visited our particular part of the country. I think his report is worthy of study by the minister and her officials. I know the director has always been very sympathetic to this type of thing.
We are having a great deal of difficulty in our municipalities which adjoin reservations-some reservations are within the boundaries of municipalities. I know that at the moment there is some litigation in this respect, and I feel sure the minister will give this matter study. I think very worthwhile advances have been made also in providing direction, and sometimes equipment, for the processing of lumber from the timber that is available on the reserves to aid the Indian to build for himself better accommodation. This move has certainly been worthwhile in our territory, and I think it could be extended. I wondered to what extent similar consideration is being given to directing Indians, and even providing them with certain of the basic equipment, in connection with fish processing.
In northern Ontario, according to my experience, most of the Indians today are at the mercy of the commercial fish brokers because they are not acquainted with some of the more modern methods of fish processing. I think some of the more basic equipment that is now available, and which is not expensive, as well as some advice on fish processing would have the result of giving the Indians better returns from their labours in catching fish. As a result of this lack of knowledge, and this lack of certain basic processing equipment, today the Indians are at the mercy of the fish merchants. Of course, if the Indian received a greater return there would be a benefit in the reduction of the welfare item. I think the same kind of attention ought to be given to this fish 

processing problem as has been given, in recent times, to the processing of lumber. I hope that will be done.
There are a great many difficulties, as I say, experienced by the municipalities. I must say I have found the department most sympathetic to these difficulties. I would only complain that I think, in some instances, inasmuch as we are able to rectify some things here, there may be some slight lack of knowledge on the part of the local agencies as to what is the desire in this respect. I am not one who believes, in so far as welfare and health matters are concerned, that the Indian who leaves the reserve is, forever and a day, a ward of the federal government. I think that might be a bar to integration. However, I am a great believer in a sympathetic attitude on the part of the department during what I might call the bridge stage when one would be moving from the reserve into the other type of life that would be lived normally by other Canadians. I believe that is the view of the director and, I am sure, of the minister. I just hope that it will be taken by municipalities and others who are constantly passing the buck and saying "once an Indian, always an Indian". It takes weeks sometimes for welfare and health situations to be taken care of. I hope there will be some more authority and conference provided to the local agencies so that they can deal with these things on the spot.

The matter of fish supervisors does not properly come under this item but, nevertheless, if the hon. member will make available to the department his requests in this respect we shall see whether we can comply with them. The department is always ready and willing to aid with whatever equipment will make it possible for the Indians to pursue their particular activities with greater efficiency. The supervisors will be glad to co-operate. If the hon. member has some specific suggestions to make or if he wants more supervisors in the operation of fishing and the gathering and marketing of fish, we shall be glad to do what we can to help him.

I think in the larger lakes it can be provided without very much expense. I am thinking of lakes north of Sioux Lookout and Red Lake. I think that either by loan or gift certain filleting and other types of processing equipment could be provided. If that were done I think the Indian would soon have a very much greater return per pound for the work he has put in to catch the fish in the first place.

We have assisted the Indians at Sandy lake in their goldeye program

and we shall be glad to assist any others who would like to benefit by the advice of the supervisors.

It may be that it is under this item that the question of the revolving fund comes, or does it come under the Department of Finance? I wonder whether the minister could indicate where this revolving fund could be dealt with.
We can discuss it under this item.

Very well. I do not know what has been the experience of the Indians applying for a loan under the revolving fund within the last year, but at least prior to that time many that I know of had a sad experience in trying to borrow money from the revolving fund for purposes which they thought-and in many instances I agreed with them-were ones for which loans should be made. As I say, I do not know from any personal knowledge how this fund has worked in the past year. However, the operation of it can mean a great deal to individual Indians or to groups of Indians who may want to perform some work on a farm, buy additional industrial equipment for logging, as some of them do, for fishing, for some other pursuit or even for the establishment of a store on the reserve. In years past the experience has been that it has been most difficult to get money out of the department from this revolving fund.
As the minister knows, Indians are in a most difficult position in respect of borrowing money from a bank because of the question of collateral. Those of us who are at the moment in the upper brackets of income have no difficulty in going to the bank and borrowing, say, $1,000. But an Indian would find it almost impossible to borrow money from the bank. Generally speaking, the only source from which he can get a loan is the revolving fund. I think that if there were to be a relaxation with respect to the granting of loans from the revolving fund it would certainly do a great deal so far as fishermen are concerned in the way of assisting them in getting out of the clutches of some of the fishing companies they work for. They get tied hand and foot to a fishing company, renting a boat, renting their gear, renting everything and buying everything from a particular company. They wind up at the end of the year to find that they still owe money to the company and they start off the next fishing season in precisely the same position of being in debt. I wonder whether the minister could indicate what are the general requirements for borrowing money from the revolving fund; what amount of money is in there at the present time; what
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration is the limit that any one individual may borrow, if there is any; and what is the total limit on the amount that may be borrowed from this fund.

The main requirements are character and a reasonable ability to repay. I thank the minister very much for saying that and my friend from Port Arthur for raising the matter, because we have a problem in British Columbia with respect to trap lines being ruined in this way. This has been the case for quite a

No. I am sure the hon. lady would like to tell us a little about the film board.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of those divisions of the government which is interesting and whose activities are complex. At a total additional cost of $92,380 this year, the board will be increasing during the present year the number of foreign versions of its films and will provide the deferred replacement prints for film libraries operated by the Canadian posts abroad, together with additional copies of new releases, and will supply a basic library for two new Canadian posts at Kuala Lumpur, capital of Malaya, and at Accra, the capital of Ghana.
The board has strengthened its science film division and wishes to increase by $31,500 its allotment of funds, bringing its budget up to $95,230.
Finally, the board wishes to commence the survey of 60 million feet of film held at Pendleton airport, 40 million feet of which is on cellulose nitrate base, an extremely hazardous substance. In the footage held in a hanger at Pendleton airport, in edited or unedited form, are materials from world wars I and II, the Canadian motion picture bureau, plus numerous miscellaneous accessions from government departments and others. The survey for which $20,000 is allocated will determine which portion of the material must be transferred over a period of years to film with an acetate base and also which part of it must be maintained as part of Canada's permanent historical records on film.
With respect to the distribution activities of the board, I should like to inform the house that during the fiscal year 1957-58 the board, through Canadian posts and film libraries, reached an audience of 21,008,919. Canadian films are being shown daily by the national film board in the Canadian pavilion at the Brussels fair. Approximately
3.000	visitors a day attend screenings in the 280-seat theatre operated by the national film board in the Canadian pavilion. In Canada in the last year, through the co-operation of 496 community film councils and other national and local voluntary associations and on the film board's own circuits
32.000	showings have taken place. In the northern territories and the Arctic alone the board has distributed, through the co-opera^ tion of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Department of Transport, 4,500 films. These figures do not take into account the mass audience
[The Chairman.]

which has seen national film board productions over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation national network or on private stations through local bookings.

I have one or two observations I should like to make about the film board. I am not going to embarrass the hon. lady by asking whether she thinks the film board is efficient but I do want to say a word about the subject she first mentioned in her observations, the preservation of old film going back to the first world war. If I caught the purport of the hon. lady's observations correctly, it is the intention of the present administration to preserve all of this valuable historical material that can be preserved. I am afraid from what I learned that there is some of it in such a state that this may be very difficult.
It will be edited.

I know I had some little difficulty persuading a hardhearted treasury board to make provision for starting this work and I hope the hon. lady is as successful with the present Minister of Finance as I was with his predecessor because I think in the future this is going to be one of the real treasures of our country. As to the film board itself, I think the hon. member for Dollard, in whose constituency the film board is now situated, would like to make a few observations. I do not intend to make any except to say that there is an apparent increase in the estimates of $239,000 and I was not sure that I caught the reasons for that increase.

As a matter of fact, I started to speak about the foreign versions of films and I am afraid I overlooked the introductory remarks which would have explained it. The amount requested this year is $4,258,918 which is a net increase of $239,230, of which $152,562 is required to cover the increased cost of maintaining existing activities at the level of last year and $143,880 of which represents the cost of extension of activities and new projects. I enumerated the new projects. The difference is unrequired new building vote.

Mr. Chairman, I find myself in a most difficult position tonight in discussing the estimates of the national film board. As I am still a bachelor I hate the idea of arguing with a lady, and being convinced that the national film board is doing good work for the Canadian people and for Canada it is hard for me to find room for criticism. But having in mind what the hon. lady said a few years ago in the house, that despite the fact that she was a woman she

would not ask for any quarter, I feel very much at ease in discussing the film board, and also because I have in mind that there is always room for improvement. Before making the few remarks I wish to make, I should like to ask the minister why we were not able to obtain the annual report of the film board for the year 1956-57 until today.

I understand there was some difficulty about the 1956-57 report. It was tabled, as the hon. member may know, on October 21, 1957, by the acting minister of the department. The responsibility for printing and delivering the report rests with the queen's printer. I do not know where the distribution fell down but in any event the report is available and can be procured by any member.
Was it tabled in manuscript form?
No, it was tabled in printed form.

I should like to pursue my remarks in French and I hope the minister will forgive me.
(Translation) :
It was on September 24, 1956, that the new national film board building was officially opened in Montreal, more exactly in the city of St. Laurent. On that occasion, we had the honour of playing host in Montreal and in the city of St. Laurent to federal and provincial government officials and to representatives of universities and colleges all over Canada. It was a great honour for my constituency of Dollard, and for the people of Montreal island.
All present at the opening were greatly impressed.
As member for Dollard, I must say that, when I looked at the national film board report for 1955-56, I felt proud of the frontispiece showing a picture of the new building, against the background of the city of St. Laurent and the constituency of Dollard.
At the opening of the NFB building his worship Mayor Cousineau, of St. Laurent, congratulated the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), then minister of citizenship and immigration who was responsible for the NFB in this house, for having transferred the film board to the city of St. Laurent and for having caused this magnificent building to be put up with the co-operation of the minister of transport. These events took place in 1956. But then in 1958, this
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration mayor of St. Laurent, Mr. Cousineau, became an official candidate of the party of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and this time complained of the national film board being there and even indicated to the people of the constituency of Dollard that it was a charge on the municipality.
I then told the people of Dollard that nothing could be farther from the truth. On my arrival in this house, at the very beginning of the session, I put a question on the order paper asking what advantage could accrue to the city of St. Laurent from the fact that the national film board was situated there. I was told that in 1956 the national film board had paid $23,075 to the city of St. Laurent, in lieu of taxes, and $128,807 in 1957. I was also told that in future the city of St. Laurent would receive an annual payment of $130,000.
(Text):
I wanted to bring this to the attention of the committee, Mr. Chairman, because it reminded me of the fuss made by the Conservative opposition in 1954 when it was decided by the Liberal government to move the national film board to Montreal, and more particularly to St. Laurent in the constituency of Dollard. In spite of the criticism of some members of the Conservative party, the move was authorized and the new building opened its doors in the fall of 1956, as I just said in French.
The film board had to be located in a large cultural centre not too far from the capital city, where transportation facilities were available, having in mind the bilingual status of Canada, and in a place where cultural and creative talents were easily available in the two official languages of Canada. As stated in the report of the national film board for the year 1955-56, and I quote:
The building site was chosen after 21 sites had been carefully investigated, not only with regard to transportation, proximity to residential areas, utilities, soil conditions and other pertinent factors, but also with special consideration for such relevant conditions as ground vibration, noise levels and atmospheric contamination. Sound and vibration tests were carried out with jet aircraft overhead, heavy trucks on the highway and diesel trains on the neighbouring railway-all conditions common to metropolitan areas.
The government of that day found no better place than Montreal to meet the requirements I have just outlined. I was glad that St. Laurent, situated in the constituency of Dollard, was chosen as the site of the national film board. If the people of Canada now have reason to be proud of the beautiful
4260	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration building which houses the board, we in Dollard are very proud to have that board in our district. In its new building the board carries on the good job it has been doing since its creation. The working conditions are ideal.
It is stated in the annual report of the national film board for 1955-56, and I quote:
New quarters, to house the board's equipment and staff once the move was over, were specially designed to meet the necessities of film-making under modern conditions, including colour, wide screen techniques and television requirements. Every measure was taken to ensure that the installations in the new building were adequate for the program of the board and technically up to date in all possible respects.
When it was decided to build the $6 million building for the film board, we were accused as usual by the Conservatives of waste and extravagance. We realize now, once again, that the Conservative accusations came out of the blue. Those accusations of waste and extravagance have disappeared. The Conservatives, now in office, have just awarded a contract to a Montreal firm for a $350,000 addition to the national film board building. I am glad to see that the present minister is aware of the importance of the national film board, and its needs, if it is to discharge its responsibilities to the satisfaction of the people of Canada.
We owe the present building to the foresight of Messrs. Winters, Harris and Pickersgill. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate attended the opening of the national film board as the representative of the government. The people who met him on that occasion remember him as a man of foresight, action, devotion to duty and a great Canadian.
As stated in the annual report for 1956-57, at page 3,
Now, for the first time in its 17-year span of operations the combined facilities of the board- production, technical operations, administration and distribution branches-are located under the one roof.
Almost 500 people, many of them skilled technicians and craftsmen, are employed in the new building. In the spring of 1957, Mr. Guy Roberge was appointed government film commissioner and chairman of the national film board. Under his able direction the national film board in its new building has taken advantage of its many facilities and has done an outstanding job. Under Mr. Roberge's direction the morale of the national film board and of its employees has never been so high.
In the past year the film board has produced, to my knowledge, outstanding films. I should like at this time to commend the national film board for its production of the


film entitled "The Sceptre and the Mace" which was a report of the royal visit of 1957. This production, which has been seen by millions of people, is further proof of the high skill of the people of the national film board.
I should like also to mention the films produced under the direction of Mr. Norman MacLaren, who is, I should say, one of the best ambassadors Canada has. From what I know and from what I have heard, his films are known and admired all across the world and have been awarded prizes at many European festivals. I sincerely hope that the minister and the government will see fit to continue providing the national film board with all the facilities possible to enable them to do their job and achieve the aims and objects which have been assigned to that board. It is my strong belief that Canada cannot do without a body like the national film board. Again, I wish to say how happy I am to have the national film board in my constituency. I hope that the present minister will find it convenient to visit the building before long.
I may add that I would be pleased on that occasion to show her around the surroundings of the film board, that is, St. Laurent and the constituency of Dollard. I am quite convinced that her charms will conquer the hearts of our people. If I am not eager to see her at election time, I will be very happy to see her in my riding in between elections.

I have only a word to say about the film board. I should like to congratulate the board, through the minister, on the work it is doing and especially, if I may say so, upon its contribution to the projection of Canada abroad.
I have had some experience with the results of that work and they are admirable. The board that has done that work has done a great deal to make Canada known abroad and in the right way.
The other matter that I want to mention was touched on by my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and it is this. I am glad to hear from the minister that the board is proceeding with the work of the preservation of these earlier war films. I am not quite sure of the technical considerations involved but I would hope that perhaps, in the relationship between the board and the C.B.C., it might be possible to show some of these films on television. The reason I say that is that, along with other members, I have been immensely interested in the series the C.B.C., is showing, I think by arrangement with the B.B.C., of British war films and American war films of the second war. If that could be done with Canadian films showing Canadian participation I think it would

be of educational value and it would be of great interest to viewers.
May I just conclude by expressing my satisfaction with the work that is being accomplished by the board.

I want to express our appreciation of the good work being done by the film board both at home and abroad. I can wholeheartedly support the complimentary remarks made by the previous speakers in this discussion. However, I do not want to take up the time of the house by repetition. I want to bring to the attention of the minister and of the committee one particular aspect of the film board's activities that I think have been very much worth while indeed. speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
speechtext:
The main estimates of my department, Mr. Chairman, and of the other agencies reporting to me, excluding loans, amount for the fiscal year to almost $254 million as compared with $219,750,000 the previous year. To this has been added in supplementary estimates an additional $7 million, so that the gross increase as compared with the previous year is over $41 million. The major portion of this overall increase is due to a substantial expansion of our construction program this year, designed both to meet the rapidly growing requirements of transportation and communications in this country and to assist economic conditions.
In view of the size and complexities of the department and its associated agencies, and because of the time at my disposal, I do not intend to explain the estimates in detail. However, it does seem to me that it would be helpful, and particularly so to those members attending their first session, if I were to touch upon the highlights.
In the canals branch, the level of activity will not materially change during the present year in so far as operation is concerned. We expect that towards the end of this year the mainline Ontario-St. Lawrence and great lakes canals will all be transferred for administration by the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, since otherwise two canal organizations would be functioning in the same area. As for the secondary canals, such as the Rideau, Trent, Chambly and the Canso, we will continue our efforts to improve these both in facilities and in attractiveness as a means of serving the growing popularity of boating, domestic and tourist.
We are doing everything we can to find employment for those individuals who have been displaced by the flooding of a number of the Ontario-St. Lawrence canals consequent upon the opening of the seaway. Preferential treatment is being given in connection with work on the seaway and on certain of our other canals, and we hope that a large proportion of the individuals concerned can be offered alternative employment.
In the field of canal construction we have increased our program by $2 million or over 100 per cent. This expenditure is spread over a large number of small projects, but there are certain large items which merit attention. These include improvement of the Canso canal by installation of fenders and extension of the mooring wall; the initial funds required to start on the long delayed project of cleaning up the old, disused second 57071-3-270
Supply-Transport
Welland canal; two causeways to connect the main highway with the village of Cardinal across the old Williamsburg canal; continuation of the work on the new bridge across the Lachine canal at Ville St. Pierre.
As for the Chjgnecto canal project, previous economic studies have indicated doubt as to whether the benefits that would result from the project would offset its very heavy costs. Notwithstanding this, we have recently asked the Department of Pubic Works to give us a preliminary engineering estimate on the cost of the Chignecto project, on the basis of which I propose to have a further economic study made and to report my findings to my colleagues.
Staff requirements in this area of operation have not varied substantially, but there is an increase in our wage and salary requirements due to salary increases.
Turning to marine services, I should note in passing that there has been an extensive reorganization of the marine sections of my department which has resulted in three separate branches being established. One branch is charged with all regulatory matters in the marine field arising out of the Canada Shipping Act, such as nautical services, pilotage and steamship inspection; a second branch is charged with the provision of marine aids, such as lights and buoys, harbour administration, supervision of the secondary canals and the St. Lawrence ship channel; and a third branch is charged with construction and operation of departmental vessels, including our icebreaking program and Arctic patrol and supply work. This reorganization has been made necessary by the rapid growth of our activities in the marine field in recent years.
Our requirements for operation of our departmental vessels are substantially increased over last year. We will have a couple of new vessels to put into service this year, although the main impact of our new vessel construction program will not make itself felt until later years. Our vessels not only perform winter icebreaking duties and summer Arctic patrol icebreaking and convoy duties, but they are used for the placing and supply of our various aids to navigation in coastal and inland waters, a very extensive task. We do have substantial increases in our requirements for the charter of commercial vessels for northern and Arctic supply, and for provision of stevedoring services and ship-to-shore equipment for lightering barges in the Arctic. These are required because of our general responsibility in providing marine supply for civil departments of government, for the R.C.A.F.

Supply-Transport
buildings and the extension of existing structures; construction of entirely new airports and installation of special facilities such as runway and approach lighting systems, power plants, heating plants, barracks, garages, etc.
We have recently completed a ten-year analysis of expected airport and airfield construction needs in Canada and, based on that analysis, the figure included in this year's budget represents the approximate amount we may be required to expend annually over the next ten years if we are to keep abreast of aviation requirements.
There are also the usual items relating to grants for small municipal airstrips-either outright grants or those on a cost sharing basis. Our policy in this regard is under review and I am not in a position to make a definite statement as yet but it may be necessary to increase the existing ceiling in respect of the amount of a grant while at the same time making the prerequisites somewhat more stringent.
Hitherto we have made grants up to $25,000 when a municipality is willing to provide the land and to operate the field. If amounts in excess of this are needed for a small local airstrip we provide additional funds on a cost sharing basis with the municipality. I am inclined to think that in future we should make slightly larger grants when satisfied that an important local need involving the federal government exists, such as service to a remote community dependent upon air transportation, but that in other cases, where a small airstrip may be beneficial but not essential we should insist on cost sharing from the outset. However, the final outlines of this policy have not yet been determined.
Our assistance to flying training continues to represent a successful part of our program. We have for many years been paying $100 to the club or school which provides the training and $100 to the pilot, in the case of each person who learns to fly, which has led to a gradual but steady increase in pilot training. The number of student pilots being trained roughly eight years ago was 1,200 annually. This had increased a year or so ago to 1,600, and we expect that it should pass 2,000 this year.
There are many other points in connection with the departmental activities upon which I could comment at this time. I trust, however, that the foregoing will be of some assistance to hon. members in dealing with my estimates. I would remind the committee that we have spent many hours in a special committee of this house in examining my estimates in greater detail and have heard evidence from a large number of the officials

of the department and other agencies. I trust that the exhaustive inquiry which took place during those sessions will be borne in mind by hon. members in dealing with the estimates in this committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
First, Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the Minister of Transport for the very comprehensive statement he has made concerning the various activities of his department. Anyone listening to that statement from an unbiased standpoint cannot help but come to the conclusion that the Department of Transport is responsible for varied activities in the field of transportation.
I should also like to congratulate the minister upon his appointment to this department because I believe this is the first time any one of us has had an opportunity to do so, since there was no occasion during the last session of parliament to consider either the activities of his department or the estimates themselves. I congratulate the hon. gentleman not only because of the position he holds but more particularly because of the department over which he presides. I may perhaps have a preference for it but I have no hesitation in saying to the minister as well as to the members of this committee that among the portfolios in the government there is none in my opinion that is better than the one over which the minister presides. That is why I think he is fortunate in being the minister of this department which is not only extremely important but also extremely interesting.
I should like to add to that a word about those officers-those faithful officers-of the Department of Transport whom he has to serve him and assist him. I know something of their devotion to duty and their loyalty because of my association with them for a period of over nine years and I can therefore speak with some authority. That is why I am happy this evening to say to the minister that he is fortunate in the calibre of these men, and that in these men and women he is extremely well served in the Department of Transport.
Having said that, and realizing that the minister has already referred to the fact that these estimates have been given some consideration in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, I will not detain the committee unduly. I did have some remarks to make which were of an extensive character, but because of the fact that there was some consideration given to these estimates in the committee and because, also, of the fact that we are in the dying days of this session I do not intend to speak at length. I think I can finish what I have to

say before ten o'clock, and if I do not, I wish the minister would stop me.
I do want, however, this evening to deal with a special aspect of transportation. It is one which has to do with the province from which I come and which I represent. It has to do with the Lachine section of the St. Lawrence river and I would make a special appeal to the minister to give consideration to the treatment which I believe the province of Quebec is entitled to receive with reference to the development of the Lachine section. There has not before, I believe, been any consideration, of this aspect of the St. Lawrence seaway. That has been the case because, I think, an opportunity has not arisen. But an opportunity has now arisen to speak on it and I believe that serious consideration should be given to this point not only by the Department of Transport but also by the government as a whole.
The minister may know that recently a statement was made by an official of Quebec hydro that it is the intention of that division of the Quebec government to develop power in the Lachine section of the St. Lawrence seaway. The power development can, of course, be done independently of the navigation development, but I think it was envisaged all along that there would be tremendous savings if both power and navigation in that section could be developed on a joint basis. The reason I bring this up now is that there have been given in connection with the upper reaches of the seaway substantial amounts of money for channel enlargement and for power development there, and having regard to that it strikes me that because of commitments made by the federal government in the past and because of the present situation there is an obligation on the part of the federal government to make similar contributions to the province of Quebec.
Perhaps I can make myself clear by saying that I believe the vice-president of Quebec hydro stated recently that in the near future it would be necessary to develop the Lachine section of the St. Lawrence river, and in saying that he also stated that a group of engineers had been requested to prepare preliminary plans and studies of that development. He said it would be possible in his opinion to develop Lachine on a two-stage basis, developing the one stage at the head of the Lachine rapids and the other stage below Victoria bridge in the harbour of Montreal, all of which would bring about a power development in the neighbourhood of between 900,000 and 1,000,000 horsepower. I make that statement because the Department of Transport, as the minister knows, gave careful consideration to this whole matter
Supply-Transport
when in 1947 there was established a board of engineers on the Lachine section and a report was tabled in the House of Commons. The board of engineers at that time was asked three questions: first, is the scheme for the improvement of the Lachine section, recommended by the joint board of engineers in this report of November 16, practicable; does it provide to the best advantage for the logical and planned development of this section; and, thirdly, what alternative scheme, if any, would be better adapted to secure the ends desired.
The board of engineers in conjunction with the officers of Quebec hydro gave careful consideration to this matter and they recommended three schemes; first, exclusive power development; secondly, a joint power and navigation scheme; and, thirdly, a navigation scheme alone. It was attempted at that time by the former government to convince the province of Quebec to develop power jointly with navigation, but that government was not successful in its endeavour. I have no blame to cast on anyone, because the question of power is one which belongs to the provinces, and in the final analysis it is for them and for them alone to determine what is their responsibility.
The point I am making is that the federal government proceeded with navigational facilities in the Lachine section without regard to power. In my opinion the cost for the development of power because of that will be increased by some $25 million, and it strikes me that even now, even at this late date, I should ask the minister and his department to see if it would not be possible to make some agreement with the province of Quebec whereby power and navigation could be proceeded with jointly to the advantage of both the province and the federal government.
In locating the facilities on the south shore regard was had, of course, to industrial development and regard was had particularly to the triangle which extends between Valley-field on the west, Sorel on the east and Montreal in the centre, because there is a tremendous triangle there which will benefit because of industrial development.
In the endeavour to assist the provincial authorities with reference to this aspect of the project a number of things were done at the time, not only to assist them but also to protect provincial rights. One of those was that the seaway authority determined to enlarge the cross-sectional area upstream from Lachine rapids in order to provide for easier power development when that was undertaken at a future date. Then lands were exchanged between the authority and Quebec hydro at Beauharnois in order to assist Quebec hydro

Supply-Transport
in expanding its power development there. There was also provided a canal which would take 40,000 cubic feet a second of water in order to aid in additional power development during the non-navigation season. Finally, hydraulic models were constructed at the request of the international joint commission for the use of the seaway authority as well as Quebec hydro.
The point I am trying to make is this, and I will come to it at once. Back in 1941 Mr. Mackenzie King wrote to the then premier of Quebec, Adelard Godbout, dealing with this whole matter. The letter divides itself into three parts. The first part has to do with representations from the province of Quebec-on all international boards or other boards directing the design or construction of works and that, I think, has been respected. The next had to do with the apportionment of rights and obligations arising out of the development of the Beauharnois section. I would like to read the first sentence of the third because it is of extreme importance. Mr. Mackenzie King went on to tell the Hon. Adelard God-bout, the premier of the province at that time, the following:
With this end in view, the government of Canada would be prepared to undertake that, if and when Quebec takes over the control and operation of the Beauharnois development, there will be paid to the government of Quebec, by the government of Canada, the sum of $7,972,500.
That was in 1941. Roughly speaking, that was a sum of $8 million. That sum has never been paid to the province of Quebec. At today's value of money I would think it would be the equivalent of some $20 million. The point I am trying to make is that having regard to the sums of money paid for channel development and power development in the upper sections of the St. Lawrence river, as and when the province of Quebec decides to construct and develop power in the Lachine section that province is entitled to the same treatment as given to the province which resides upstream. Having regard to the value of money today I would say that would be no less than $20 million.
I make this statement having regard to the facts with which I have prefaced my remarks and I make it, too, with this appeal to the minister. Whether the Lachine section is developed in 1958, or next year, or the year after, makes no difference. There is no doubt in my mind that it will have to be developed. It will have to be developed because of the tremendous number of industries which are coming within that triangle and power from Beauharnois will not suffice indefinitely. It
will be necessary to get additional power from Lachine and it seems to me that the Minister of Transport will play an important part in that, not only because of the facilities which he is building today with the St. Lawrence seaway but also because of the fact that legislation will be required in order to develop this power. Legislation will be required with respect to the Lachine section in the same manner as legislation was required in connection with the international section. Therefore, it was decided to enter into an agreement with the province of Ontario and the terms and conditions were clearly set out in that agreement. The same thing should appertain with reference to the development in Lachine section.
I thought I should make this point because I am sure it has already come to the attention of the minister. If it has not, it will in the near future and I know he will give it his careful attention.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to thank the hon. member for Laurier for his very constructive contribution to the debate and to assure him that we will follow his suggestion. We will be very glad to approach the province of Quebec and see whether that province will be interested in developing the power in the Lachine section at this time. I can assure him, and we will assure them, that if they are interested we will give them every co-operation in such an endeavour.

It is so close to ten o'clock I wonder whether we can call it ten o'clock.
